  findings: The paper finds that introducing local (group-level) sanctioning institutions (punishment) in threshold public goods games with risk of collective loss significantly increases the fraction of groups that successfully achieve the public good, especially under low risk perception and high contribution thresholds. Global (population-wide) sanctioning institutions provide only marginal improvement. Smaller group sizes and higher risk perception also promote higher group achievement. Threshold uncertainty (uncertainty about the required contribution level) can sharply reduce group achievement. The model suggests that decentralized, polycentric punishment is more effective than centralized punishment for promoting cooperation and group success.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides strong theoretical support that enabling punishment (specifically, local/group-level sanctioning institutions) in threshold public goods games with risk of collective loss will increase group achievement (a close proxy for efficiency), especially when group size is small, risk perception is high, and contribution thresholds are stringent. The effect of punishment is much stronger when implemented locally rather than globally. The findings suggest that, for prediction tasks, the presence of local punishment should be expected to yield a more positive effect on efficiency-related outcomes than global punishment or no punishment, particularly in small groups and under high risk. However, the main outcome is group achievement, not exact efficiency, so predictions should be interpreted accordingly.

- source: Gao, S. P., Suo, J. H., & Li, N. (2025). Cooperation under endogenous punishment in the spatial public goods game. *Applied Mathematics and Computation*.
  type: theory | empirical=N/A | experimental=N/A
  relevance: pgg=exact | punishment=exact | payoff=close
  outcomes: primary=non_payoff_behavior | overall_effect=N/A
  dimensions: player_count, all_or_nothing, mpcr, punishment_cost, punishment_tech
  findings: The paper finds that endogenous punishment can promote cooperation in spatial public goods games when the network reciprocity alone is insufficient (i.e., when the enforcement factor is below the threshold for cooperation in the absence of punishment). The effectiveness of punishment depends on the willingness of cooperators to punish (probability p), the cost and fine of punishment, and the network degree. There is a critical value of p above which cooperation can be sustained. However, when network reciprocity is already strong enough to support cooperation, adding endogenous punishment can actually hinder cooperation or have no additional effect. The evolutionary dynamics can be bi-stable, with both all-cooperator and all-defector states possible depending on initial conditions. The model provides explicit threshold formulas for when cooperation is favored.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides theoretical guidance on how endogenous punishment, punishment cost and effectiveness, and network structure interact to affect the likelihood of achieving full cooperation (and thus maximal efficiency) in spatial public goods games. While it does not report empirical efficiency values, it gives explicit formulas for the thresholds at which cooperation becomes stable or dominant, as a function of the marginal per-capita return (mpcr), punishment cost, punishment effectiveness, and network degree. For prediction tasks, the results suggest that enabling punishment can increase efficiency (by supporting all-cooperation) when the control game is below the cooperation threshold, but may have little or even negative effect when the control game already achieves high cooperation due to network reciprocity. The model is most informative for structured populations with endogenous, probabilistic punishment.

- source: Quan, J., Chu, Y. Q., Liu, W., Wang, X. J., & Yang, X. K. (2018). Stochastic evolutionary public goods game with first and second order costly punishments in finite populations. *Chinese Physics B*.
  type: theory | empirical=N/A | experimental=N/A
  relevance: pgg=exact | punishment=exact | payoff=close
  outcomes: primary=non_payoff_behavior | overall_effect=more_positive
  dimensions: player_count, all_or_nothing, mpcr, punishment_cost, punishment_tech
  findings: The paper finds that introducing first-order costly punishment into a finite-population public goods game can shift the system from an all-defection equilibrium to a coexistence of cooperation and punishment, provided that both the punishment intensity and the return on investment are large enough. This shift implies higher group welfare and efficiency, as the all-defection state is inefficient. Second-order punishment (punishing cooperators who do not punish defectors) does not dramatically change the evolutionary dynamics except in certain critical parameter combinations, and mainly increases the proportion of punishers among cooperators in coexistence states. The model provides a detailed mapping of parameter regions where cooperation is stochastically stable.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides strong theoretical support that, in finite-population public goods games, enabling costly punishment (with sufficient intensity and return on investment) can substantially increase the probability of the system being in cooperative or mixed cooperative-punisher states, which are more efficient than all-defection. The findings suggest that, for prediction tasks, the presence and strength of punishment, as well as the return on investment (mpcr), are key moderators of the efficiency gain from punishment. However, the paper does not report direct efficiency ratios, so predictions must be inferred from the stability of cooperative states. Second-order punishment adds little except in narrow parameter regions. The results are most applicable to settings matching the model's assumptions (finite, well-mixed populations, no communication, discrete strategies).

- source: Lv, S. J., Zhang, X. X., Zhong, A. Y., Mi, J., & He, Q. L. (2022). Synergy and discount of punishment in the public goods game. *Physics Letters A*.
  type: theory | empirical=N/A | experimental=N/A
  relevance: pgg=exact | punishment=exact | payoff=close
  outcomes: primary=non_payoff_behavior | overall_effect=N/A
  dimensions: player_count, all_or_nothing, mpcr, punishment_cost, punishment_tech
  findings: The paper finds that nonlinear punishment (synergy or discount) significantly affects the evolutionary dynamics of cooperation in public goods games. In well-mixed populations, cooperation cannot be the unique stable equilibrium; both cooperation and defection can be stable depending on parameters and initial conditions. In structured populations (regular networks), cooperation can become the unique stable equilibrium under certain conditions. The effectiveness of punishment (synergy parameter), group size, network degree, and punishment severity all interact to determine whether cooperation is promoted. Synergistic punishment (increasing effectiveness with more punishers) can enlarge the domain of attraction for cooperation, especially in structured populations. The impact of network degree (group size) is non-monotonic and depends on the level of punishment severity. The paper provides explicit replicator equations and phase diagrams but does not report explicit efficiency or group payoff values.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides theoretical guidance on how nonlinear punishment mechanisms, group size, network structure, and punishment severity interact to affect the evolutionary stability of cooperation in public goods games. While it does not report explicit efficiency or group payoff outcomes, it shows that synergistic punishment and certain network structures can make cooperation more stable, which would likely increase group efficiency in practice. The findings suggest that, for prediction tasks, the presence of synergistic punishment, lower punishment costs, and structured populations (as opposed to well-mixed) are likely to increase the efficiency gains from enabling punishment. However, the lack of explicit efficiency or payoff data limits direct quantitative prediction.

- source: Greenwood, G. W., Abbass, H. A., & Petraki, E. (2018). When is altruistic punishment useful in social dilemmas?. *Biosystems*.
  type: theory | empirical=N/A | experimental=N/A
  relevance: pgg=exact | punishment=exact | payoff=close
  outcomes: primary=non_payoff_behavior | overall_effect=mixed
  dimensions: player_count, all_or_nothing, mpcr, punishment_cost, punishment_tech
  findings: The paper finds that altruistic punishment in a public goods game is only effective at promoting cooperation (and thus improving group outcomes) if the frequency of punishers exceeds a threshold determined by the cost of contribution and the punishment level. If this threshold is not met, defection remains the dominant strategy and group efficiency does not improve. The analysis provides explicit formulas for the returns to each strategy and the minimum frequency of punishers required for punishment to be effective. The findings imply that simply enabling punishment is not sufficient to improve efficiency; the population composition and punishment parameters are critical.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides strong theoretical guidance for predicting when punishment will improve efficiency in public goods games. It shows that the effect of punishment on efficiency is conditional: punishment only increases efficiency if the proportion of punishers is above a threshold that depends on the cost of contribution and the punishment level. For prediction tasks, this means that the presence of punishment does not guarantee higher efficiency; the effectiveness depends on the game parameters (contribution cost, punishment cost/impact) and the frequency of punishers. The explicit formulas can be used to estimate the required conditions for punishment to be effective, but the paper does not provide empirical efficiency values or group payoff data.

- source: Xia, C. Y., Zhang, J. J., Wang, Y. L., & Wang, J. S. (2011). Evolution of Cooperation in Public Goods Games. *Communications in Theoretical Physics*.
  type: theory | empirical=N/A | experimental=N/A
  relevance: pgg=exact | punishment=exact | payoff=close
  outcomes: primary=mixed | overall_effect=more_positive
  dimensions: player_count, mpcr, punishment_cost, punishment_tech
  findings: The paper demonstrates, through theoretical modeling and numerical simulation, that adding punishment to voluntary public goods games in finite populations with bounded rationality increases both the frequency of cooperation and the average payoff of the group. The effect of punishment is especially strong when the loner's payoff is not too high, and the model shows that punishment can suppress defectors and promote higher payoffs for cooperators and punishers. The results are compared to both compulsory PGG and VPGG without punishment, showing that the addition of punishment leads to higher cooperation and average payoffs. The findings are robust to variations in group size, rationality parameter, and loner's payoff.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides strong theoretical support that, in public goods games with voluntary participation, enabling punishment mechanisms increases average group payoff (i.e., efficiency) compared to the same game without punishment, especially when the loner's payoff is not too high. The model explicitly includes key design dimensions such as player count, number of rounds (implicitly infinite or repeated), punishment cost and effectiveness, and the presence of loners. The results suggest that, for prediction tasks, the presence of punishment should be expected to increase efficiency, with the effect moderated by the value of the loner's payoff and the rationality parameter. The findings are most directly applicable to settings with voluntary participation, finite groups, and bounded rationality.

- source: Liu, X. S., & Guo, W. L. (2010). Persistent cooperators in nature. *Journal of Theoretical Biology*.
  type: theory | empirical=N/A | experimental=N/A
  relevance: pgg=exact | punishment=exact | payoff=close
  outcomes: primary=non_payoff_behavior | overall_effect=more_positive
  dimensions: mpcr, punishment_cost, punishment_tech
  findings: The paper finds that in a public goods game with compulsory participation, if contributors are willing to pay a second cost to retrieve a portion of the public good (persistent cooperation), this can functionally act as punishment and promote cooperation. When the second cost is not too high relative to the benefit, persistent cooperators can dominate the population, leading to higher average payoffs and more stable cooperation. The model provides explicit conditions (in terms of benefit-to-cost ratios and the size of the second cost) under which persistent cooperation is evolutionarily stable, risk-dominant, or advantageous. When the second cost is high, persistent cooperators act as traditional costly punishers and are less favored. The abundance of persistent cooperators is used as a proxy for group welfare and efficiency.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides theoretical support for the idea that punishment-like mechanisms (modeled as a second cost paid by persistent cooperators) can increase the prevalence of cooperation and, by extension, group efficiency, as long as the cost of punishment is not too high relative to the benefit. The model gives explicit parameter thresholds for when punishment is beneficial. For prediction tasks, the findings suggest that enabling punishment (with moderate cost and sufficient benefit) in a public goods game is likely to increase efficiency compared to a control without punishment, especially when the punishment cost is not excessive. The model also highlights the importance of the ratio between the benefit of cooperation, the cost of contributing, and the cost of punishment in determining the outcome. However, the paper does not provide direct quantitative predictions of efficiency, and its results are theoretical rather than empirical.

- source: Zhang, B. Y., & Pei, S. (2022). Game Theory and the Evolution of Cooperation. *Journal of the Operations Research Society of China*.
  type: theory | empirical=N/A | experimental=N/A
  relevance: pgg=exact | punishment=exact | payoff=close
  outcomes: primary=non_payoff_behavior | overall_effect=N/A
  dimensions: player_count, num_rounds, all_or_nothing, mpcr, punishment_cost, punishment_tech
  findings: The paper reviews theoretical and empirical literature on the evolution of cooperation in public goods games and related social dilemmas. It finds that punishment (both peer and institutional) can promote cooperation, especially in one-shot or non-repeated interactions, but at a cost that can reduce group welfare or average payoff. Peer punishment can curb free-riding but is costly and can lead to second-order free-riding and antisocial punishment, often resulting in lower group payoffs compared to no-punishment conditions. Institutional punishment can overcome some of these issues but is also costly. Reward mechanisms are generally less effective than punishment in moving populations from defection to cooperation, unless the reward is large. The paper emphasizes that combining reward and punishment can have a strong effect on promoting cooperation. Theoretical models predict that the effect of punishment on cooperation and payoff depends on the size and structure of the incentive, and that punishment can eliminate extremely selfish behavior but does not always increase group efficiency.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides theoretical and review-based guidance that punishment mechanisms in public goods games can increase cooperation rates, but often at a cost that may reduce group efficiency or average payoff, especially in peer punishment settings. The effect of punishment on efficiency is not universally positive and depends on the cost and effectiveness of punishment, as well as the structure of the game (e.g., peer vs institutional punishment, compulsory vs voluntary participation). For prediction tasks, the paper suggests that enabling punishment is likely to increase cooperation but may not always increase efficiency, and in some cases may reduce it due to the costs of punishment. The paper does not provide quantitative estimates or new empirical data, so its value is mainly in providing qualitative, mechanism-based expectations and summarizing prior findings.

- source: Shen, Y., Guo, J., & Kang, H. W. (2024). The Influence of Fine Distribution and Compensation on Cooperation in Public Goods Game. *Mathematics*.
  type: theory | empirical=N/A | experimental=N/A
  relevance: pgg=exact | punishment=exact | payoff=adjacent
  outcomes: primary=non_payoff_behavior | overall_effect=N/A
  dimensions: player_count, num_rounds, all_or_nothing, mpcr, punishment_cost, punishment_tech
  findings: The study shows that introducing probabilistic punishment into a spatial public goods game increases the prevalence of cooperation compared to the baseline. Adding fine distribution (punishers receive a share of fines from defectors) and compensation (punishers compensate cooperators when punishment fails) further increases the prevalence and stability of cooperation, especially across a broader range of punishment costs and intensities. The compensation mechanism is most effective at low punishment costs, while fine distribution is most effective at high punishment costs. The main outcome is the fraction of cooperators, not group efficiency or total payoff.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides strong evidence that probabilistic punishment, fine distribution, and compensation mechanisms can increase the prevalence of cooperation in spatial public goods games. However, because the reported outcomes are cooperation rates rather than efficiency or group payoff, the findings should be used with caution for predicting efficiency effects. The results suggest that, under similar game design dimensions (e.g., spatial structure, probabilistic punishment, fine distribution, compensation), enabling punishment is likely to increase cooperation rates, which may be associated with higher efficiency in many PGG contexts, but this is not directly demonstrated. The paper is most informative for predicting the direction and robustness of cooperation rate changes, not for quantitative efficiency predictions.

  findings: The simulation results show that both punishment and reward mechanisms increase the fraction of knowledge contributors compared to no incentive, but punishment is more effective than reward. Mixed mechanisms (punishment plus reward) are less effective than either alone. The relationship between fine/bonus size and knowledge sharing is nonlinear: moderate fines/bonuses maximize knowledge sharing, while very high or low values are less effective. Peer pressure, time pressure, and coworkers' attitudes significantly affect knowledge sharing rates. The main outcome is the behavioral rate of knowledge sharing, not group efficiency or total payoff.

The results are based on agent-based simulations, not empirical data. The findings are most useful for predicting changes in contribution rates, not efficiency. The model details (e.g., player count, network structure, incentive parameters) are informative for mapping to design dimensions, but the lack of direct efficiency or payoff outcomes limits the paper's value for predicting treatment efficiency from control efficiency and design dimensions.

  findings: The study demonstrates that in a continuous SPGG with punishment, the use of exploration-based particle swarm optimization (EPSO) and its parameter optimization via Q-learning (QPSO) can rapidly drive the system to a state of full cooperation (ACI=1) under certain parameter regimes. Both low and high values of the individual learning coefficient (c1), higher inertia weight (omega), lower punishment intensity (eta), and higher gain intensity (r) promote higher cooperation intensity. The main reported outcome is ACI, not direct group payoff or efficiency. The findings are based on simulation experiments with large populations (L=200, i.e., 40,000 agents) on a square lattice, and the results are robust across a range of parameter values.

The results suggest that, in similar simulation/theoretical models, enabling punishment with low punishment intensity and high gain intensity can drive the system to near-full cooperation, which would likely correspond to high efficiency if mapped to payoff outcomes. However, the lack of direct efficiency or payoff reporting limits the direct applicability to the prediction task. The findings are most relevant for understanding how parameter settings (punishment intensity, gain intensity, learning coefficients) modulate the effect of punishment on cooperation, which may inform priors for efficiency outcomes in similar game designs.

  type: theory | empirical=N/A | experimental=N/A

  dimensions: player_count, num_rounds, all_or_nothing, mpcr, punishment_cost, punishment_tech
  findings: The study uses agent-based simulations of a spatial public goods game on a square lattice, where each player participates in five overlapping groups. The key manipulation is the introduction of a symmetric, mutual punishment: whenever two neighbors have different strategies, both pay a punishment fine. The main result is that higher punishment fines lead to higher steady-state cooperation rates, and for sufficiently high fines, the population becomes fully cooperative. The mechanism is robust to changes in system size and noise. The paper provides a formula for the payoff difference between cooperators and defectors at the interface between clusters, showing that this difference increases with the punishment fine, favoring the spread of cooperation. However, the paper does not report group-level efficiency or total payoff, so the effect on efficiency is not directly established.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides strong evidence that mutual punishment increases cooperation rates in spatial public goods games, especially as the punishment fine increases. However, because the paper does not report group efficiency, total payoff, or welfare, it does not directly inform the prediction of efficiency outcomes. The findings are most useful for predicting changes in cooperation rates, not efficiency. The model is theoretical and does not include communication, reward, or other institutional features. The punishment is symmetric and always applied when strategies differ, which is a specific variant of punishment not always present in experimental or real-world settings.

- source: Thöni, C. (2014). Inequality aversion and antisocial punishment. *Theory and Decision*.
  type: theory | empirical=N/A | experimental=N/A

  outcomes: primary=non_payoff_behavior | overall_effect=N/A
  dimensions: player_count, num_rounds, all_or_nothing, mpcr, punishment_cost, punishment_tech
  findings: The paper shows that, while inequality aversion can theoretically motivate antisocial punishment under certain conditions, empirical data from several public goods game experiments indicate that most antisocial punishment acts do not fit this explanation. Instead, antisocial punishment is often carried out by the richest group members and is not typically accompanied by punishment of free riders, contrary to the predictions of the inequality aversion model. The findings suggest that other motives, such as revenge or a desire to harm others, are more likely explanations for antisocial punishment. The paper does not provide direct evidence on efficiency or group payoff, but notes that antisocial punishment is detrimental to the efficiency of informal punishment mechanisms.
  prediction_guidance: This paper is useful for understanding the behavioral mechanisms behind antisocial punishment in public goods games with punishment, but it does not provide direct quantitative evidence on the effect of punishment on efficiency or group payoff. It does, however, reinforce the point that the presence and frequency of antisocial punishment can undermine the positive effects of punishment on cooperation and efficiency, especially in environments where antisocial punishment is prevalent. For prediction tasks, the paper suggests that game design features or subject pool characteristics that foster antisocial punishment may reduce or even reverse the efficiency gains from enabling punishment. However, the paper does not report efficiency or payoff outcomes directly, so it cannot be used to calibrate quantitative predictions of efficiency changes.

The model assumes infinite populations and evolutionary dynamics, which may differ from finite, repeated lab or field experiments. Inequity-averse defectors (IADs) can also promote cooperation by forming protective barriers around cooperators, reducing the ability of defectors to invade. The effectiveness of punishment depends on the ratio of fine to cost, the synergy factor (MPCR), and the spatial structure. However, the paper does not report on group efficiency or total payoff, so the direct effect on efficiency is not established.

The findings suggest that the design of punishment (who is targeted, how costs and fines scale) and the spatial structure of interactions are important moderators. However, because the paper does not report efficiency or group payoff, it cannot be used directly to predict the effect of punishment on efficiency. Instead, it supports the idea that punishment can change the behavioral composition of the group, which may be associated with higher efficiency in related models, but this link is not demonstrated here.

- source: Chen, T., Hu, X. Z., Wang, Y. J., & Wang, L. (2018). The effect of heterogeneous defectors on the evolution of public cooperation. *European Physical Journal B*.

  findings: The paper finds that introducing punishment mechanisms in PGGs with heterogeneous defectors can significantly increase the sum of contributions (i.e., promote cooperation), especially when the punishment inflicted on defectors is at least as large as the cost to punishers. The effect is strongest when the loss to defectors is double the cost to punishers. If the punishment is too costly for punishers relative to the loss inflicted, the mechanism fails to promote cooperation. The network structure also matters: small-world and scale-free networks allow cooperation to emerge more easily with lower punishment costs. The main outcome is the sum of contributions, not efficiency or total group payoff.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides indirect evidence that punishment can increase group contributions in PGG-like environments, especially when the punishment is effective (defector loss >= punisher cost) and when the network structure facilitates information flow. However, because the paper does not report efficiency or total group payoff, its findings should be used as indirect support for the prediction task. The results suggest that, for a given control efficiency, enabling punishment with sufficient effectiveness (high punishment impact per cost) is likely to increase group contributions, and thus may increase efficiency, especially in networked settings. The effect is sensitive to the relative cost and impact of punishment.

  findings: The paper finds that in a public goods game with punishment, the choice of updating rule (BP, DP, LD) can dramatically change the long-run frequencies of defectors, cooperators, and punishers. For the same parameter values, the birth-death process leads to a population dominated by defectors, while the death-birth process results in a majority of cooperative strategies (cooperators and punishers). Link dynamics yields intermediate results. These differences arise even in well-mixed populations and are especially pronounced when mutation rates are not negligible and when more than two strategies interact. The paper does not report group efficiency or payoff, but the shift from defector to cooperator/punisher dominance implies a likely increase in group welfare under some updating rules.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides strong theoretical evidence that the updating rule (a feature of evolutionary dynamics, not typically manipulated in lab experiments) can be a major moderator of the effect of punishment on cooperation and, by implication, on efficiency. In public goods games with punishment, the same game design (including punishment parameters) can yield very different long-run outcomes depending on the updating rule: punishment may be ineffective (defector-dominated) under one rule and highly effective (cooperator/punisher-dominated) under another. However, because the paper does not report efficiency or group payoff directly, its findings should be interpreted as indicating that the effect of punishment on efficiency is highly sensitive to the evolutionary dynamics assumed, especially in theoretical or agent-based models. For empirical prediction, this suggests caution in generalizing across studies with different evolutionary assumptions.

  findings: The study finds that in spatial public goods games, costly punishment (when fines are sufficiently high relative to costs) allows punishing cooperators to outcompete defectors and non-punishing cooperators, solving the second-order free-rider problem in structured populations. This effect is robust to small and moderate mutation rates, but high mutation rates (which mimic well-mixed conditions) restore the tragedy of the commons by enabling defectors to dominate. The presence of even tiny mutation rates can dramatically accelerate the spread of punishing cooperators by temporarily introducing defectors, which punishing cooperators can then outcompete. The main outcomes are the stationary fractions of each strategy, not direct measures of efficiency or group payoff.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides strong theoretical evidence that, in spatially structured public goods games, enabling punishment (with sufficiently high fine-to-cost ratio) can lead to the dominance of punishing cooperators and the elimination of defectors and non-punishing cooperators, especially at moderate mutation rates. While efficiency is not directly measured, the dominance of punishing cooperators is likely associated with higher group payoff than defector-dominated states. The results suggest that the effect of punishment on efficiency is highly sensitive to the structure of interactions (spatial vs. well-mixed) and to mutation rates. For prediction tasks, the presence of spatial structure, the fine-to-cost ratio, and mutation rate are critical moderators of punishment's effect on group outcomes.

  findings: The study finds that allowing punishment in public goods games shifts the critical synergy parameter (r) required for cooperation to emerge to lower values, making cooperation possible under less favorable conditions. Punishment acts as a catalyst for cooperation, even if it is used sparingly, and can stabilize cooperation below the critical point. However, punishment can also stabilize defection above the critical point if defectors reach a critical density. The system exhibits meta-stable phase transitions and hysteresis: once cooperation is established, it can persist even as conditions worsen, and vice versa. The main reported outcomes are the probabilities of cooperation and punishment, and the critical values of the synergy parameter, not direct efficiency or group payoff.

While it does not report efficiency or group payoff directly, the probability of cooperation is a strong proxy for efficiency in this context, as full cooperation would maximize group payoff. The findings suggest that, for a given game design, enabling punishment (especially if it is effective and not too costly) will increase the likelihood of high cooperation and thus higher efficiency, particularly near the critical synergy threshold. However, the paper does not provide quantitative efficiency values, so its support is indirect and best used for qualitative prediction or mechanistic understanding.

- source: Helbing, D., Szolnoki, A., Perc, M., & Szabó, G. (2010). Punish, but not too hard: how costly punishment spreads in the spatial public goods game. *New Journal of Physics*.

  findings: The study finds that in spatial public goods games, the introduction of punishing cooperators (PC) or punishing defectors (PD) can promote the spread of cooperation, but through different mechanisms. For punishing cooperators, increasing the punishment fine monotonically increases the cooperation level up to a threshold, after which non-punishing cooperators and defectors are eliminated. For punishing defectors, there is a non-monotonic (reentrant) effect: increasing the fine initially increases cooperation, but too high a fine reduces the fraction of punishing defectors, causing cooperation to collapse and the system to revert to defection. The results are presented as phase diagrams and time-evolution of strategy fractions, not as direct efficiency or group payoff measures.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides strong evidence that the presence and type of punishment mechanism, as well as the punishment cost and fine, can have large effects on the prevalence of cooperation in spatial public goods games. However, because the outcomes are reported as fractions of strategies and cooperation level, not as group efficiency or total payoff, the findings are only indirectly informative for predicting efficiency. The results suggest that enabling punishment (especially by punishing cooperators) can increase cooperation and likely efficiency, but the relationship is mediated by the spatial structure and the specific punishment parameters. The non-monotonic effect for punishing defectors highlights the importance of tuning punishment severity. For prediction tasks, this paper supports the idea that punishment can improve efficiency in structured populations, but the mapping to efficiency must be inferred from cooperation levels.

- source: Ding, R., Wang, X. J., Quan, J., Ma, S. T., & Zhao, J. H. (2025). The evolution of cooperation and punishment in spatial public goods games with bribery. *Chaos Solitons & Fractals*.

  findings: The study finds that in spatial public goods games with peer punishment, the introduction of bribery (defectors bribing punishers to avoid sanctions, and punishers accepting bribes) leads to complex phase transitions among strategies. When punishment intensity is low, bribery can increase the fraction of contributors (interpreted as higher cooperation), as bribe-recipients and bribers form alliances that resist defectors. As the bribe amount increases, the system can enter cyclic coexistence states involving bribers, bribe-recipients, and defectors. When punishment intensity is high, bribery undermines the maintenance of punishment and can reduce the contribution level. The effect of bribery is highly sensitive to the synergy coefficient (analogous to MPCR), punishment fine, and bribe amount. However, the paper does not report group efficiency or total payoff, focusing instead on the prevalence of strategies and contribution rates.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides indirect evidence about how punishment and bribery mechanisms interact to affect cooperation in spatial PGGs, but does not directly inform predictions about efficiency or group payoff. The findings suggest that the effect of punishment on cooperation (and by proxy, efficiency) is moderated by the possibility of bribery and the parameters of the game (synergy coefficient, punishment fine, bribe amount). In environments where punishment is weak, bribery can increase cooperation; where punishment is strong, bribery can undermine it. However, since efficiency is not directly measured, these results should be used cautiously for predicting efficiency outcomes. The model is also spatial and evolutionary, which may differ from typical lab PGGs.

- source: Hua, S. J., & Liu, L. J. (2023). Facilitating the evolution of cooperation through altruistic punishment with adaptive feedback. *Chaos Solitons & Fractals*.
  type: theory | empirical=N/A | experimental=N/A

  dimensions: player_count, num_rounds, all_or_nothing, mpcr, punishment_cost, punishment_tech
  findings: The paper finds that introducing adaptive feedback in punishment intensity—where punishment increases as defection rises and decreases as cooperation rises—can facilitate the evolution and maintenance of cooperation in public goods games. The system can exhibit bistability (converging to either full cooperation with low punishment or full defection with high punishment), stable oscillations between cooperation and defection, or stable full cooperation/defection depending on the average per capita incentive and other parameters. Notably, full cooperation can be achieved and maintained with only low-intensity punishment under certain conditions. The findings are based on theoretical analysis and numerical simulations of the replicator dynamics with feedback, not on empirical or experimental data. The paper does not report efficiency or group payoff, so implications for efficiency must be inferred indirectly.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides theoretical evidence that adaptive, feedback-based punishment can promote and stabilize cooperation in public goods games, sometimes with only low punishment intensity. While it does not report efficiency or group payoff, the results suggest that under certain parameter regimes, adaptive punishment could lead to high efficiency (if cooperation is high and punishment costs are low). However, the absence of direct efficiency analysis means that predictions about efficiency effects must be made cautiously and indirectly, based on the reported cooperation dynamics. The model is most relevant for settings with institutional punishment, adaptive feedback, and infinite well-mixed populations, and less directly applicable to finite, experimental, or empirical settings.

  findings: The study finds that introducing a modified pool punishment mechanism and aspiration-driven updating in a multi-heterogeneity public goods game on a lattice can promote cooperation under certain conditions. Specifically, moderate punishment and low aspiration factor are most effective at increasing the fraction of cooperators. Too high punishment or aspiration factor leads to instability or loss of cooperation. The results are robust to different lattice sizes and initial conditions. While average payoffs for cooperators and defectors are reported, the main focus is on cooperation rates, not group efficiency.

However, because the main outcome is cooperation rate and not group efficiency or total payoff, the findings should be used with caution for predicting efficiency. The results suggest that the effect of punishment on efficiency may be non-monotonic: moderate punishment may improve outcomes, but excessive punishment can reduce both cooperation and payoffs. The lattice structure and aspiration-driven updating are important contextual factors.

  findings: The introduction of a limited punishment pool in a public goods game can effectively suppress defectors and promote cooperation, especially when the pool's capacity is set within an optimal range. If the punishment pool is too small, defectors persist; if it is too large, punishers crowd out cooperators. The model shows that the right balance in punishment pool capacity maximizes the prevalence of cooperation. The paper does not directly report efficiency or group payoff, but notes that the 'overall income' is higher in certain parameter ranges where both cooperators and punishers coexist and defectors are suppressed.

The findings suggest that the effect of punishment on efficiency may depend on the capacity of the punishment pool: too little punishment is ineffective, but too much can reduce cooperation by crowding out cooperators. For prediction tasks, the results imply that the design of the punishment mechanism (especially its capacity and cost parameters) is crucial for maximizing cooperation, but the lack of direct efficiency or payoff data limits quantitative prediction.

  findings: The model demonstrates that the effectiveness and efficiency of central power (e.g., the Rule of Law) determine the prevalence of antisocial punishment in a population, while prosocial punishment remains stable. Antisocial punishment is highest at intermediate levels of central power and suppressed when central power is either very strong or very weak. The population can be decomposed into three basic types (Collaboration Enthusiast, Fence Sitter, Rational Bystander), and the central power shifts the proportions of these types, which in turn determines the observed punishment and contribution behaviors. The model is validated at the 'phenomenal level' by comparison to cross-regional experimental data, but does not directly report efficiency or group payoff.

However, it does not provide direct evidence on efficiency or group payoff, so it cannot be used to quantitatively predict the effect of punishment on efficiency given game design dimensions and control efficiency. It is most useful for predicting how changes in central authority or social norms might shift the prevalence of antisocial punishment and, indirectly, contribution rates. For direct efficiency prediction, empirical or simulation studies that report group payoff or efficiency are needed.

- source: Moreno, S. F. G. Y., & Gutierrez-Garcia, J. O. (2018). Collective action in organizational structures. *Computational and Mathematical Organization Theory*.

  findings: The paper finds that the structure of hierarchical organizations and the design of punishment mechanisms significantly affect collective action, as measured by aggregate contribution levels. Peer-based (collegial) punishment mechanisms lead to higher contributions than supervisor-based punishment. Organizations with more hierarchical levels achieve higher contributions when supervisor-based punishment is used. Smaller organizational units (lower span of control) also foster higher contributions, especially when only the most egoistic agent is punished. The presence of any punishment mechanism increases contributions compared to no punishment. However, all results are reported in terms of contribution rates, not efficiency or group payoff.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides strong evidence that the design of punishment mechanisms (peer vs. supervisor), the number of hierarchical levels, and the span of control can substantially affect contribution rates in repeated public goods games. However, because the outcomes are reported as contribution levels rather than efficiency or group payoff, the direct predictive value for efficiency is limited. The findings suggest that, in similar agent-based or organizational settings, enabling peer punishment and structuring organizations into smaller units with more levels may increase contributions, which could correlate with higher efficiency if punishment costs are not excessive. The paper does not provide direct evidence on the net efficiency impact, especially considering the costs of punishment.

The effect of punishment intensity is nonlinear: below a threshold, it is ineffective, but above the threshold, further increases yield little additional benefit. These findings are robust across both PGG and CRD models. However, the paper does not report on efficiency, group payoff, or welfare, so the direct effect on efficiency cannot be determined.

However, because the paper does not report efficiency, group payoff, or welfare, it cannot be used directly to predict the effect of punishment on efficiency. The findings are most useful for predicting changes in cooperation rates, not payoffs. If the downstream prediction task assumes a strong link between cooperation and efficiency, these results may be indirectly informative, but caution is warranted.

- source: Kaiping, G. A., Cox, S. J., & Sluckin, T. J. (2016). Cooperation and punishment in community-structured populations with migration. *Journal of Theoretical Biology*.
  type: theory | empirical=N/A | experimental=N/A
  relevance: pgg=exact | punishment=exact | payoff=adjacent
  outcomes: primary=non_payoff_behavior | overall_effect=N/A
  dimensions: player_count, all_or_nothing, mpcr, punishment_cost, punishment_tech
  findings: The paper finds that in community-structured populations playing a linear PGG with punishment, the presence of group competition (where entire communities can replace each other based on average fitness) or fitness-based migration (where individuals are more likely to migrate if they are fitter) can sustain high levels of cooperation and punishment, suppressing defection in parameter regions where defection would otherwise dominate. Constant (random) migration does not have this effect. The transition between cooperative and defective regimes is sharper with migration, but only group competition and fitness-based migration expand the parameter space where cooperation and punishment are stable. The main reported outcomes are the frequencies of strategies, not efficiency or group payoff, but higher frequencies of cooperation and punishment imply higher group payoffs relative to defection-dominated regimes.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides indirect but informative evidence for the prediction task: in PGG-like environments with punishment, the presence of group competition or fitness-based migration mechanisms can substantially increase the prevalence of cooperation and punishment, and thus are likely to increase efficiency or group payoff compared to control games without punishment. However, the paper does not report efficiency or group payoff directly, so the evidence is based on the frequencies of cooperative and punishing strategies. The results suggest that, for the same game design dimensions, enabling punishment in a context with group competition or fitness-based migration will likely lead to higher efficiency than in well-mixed or constant migration settings. The findings are most relevant for models with large group sizes, high mutation and migration rates, and community structure.

  findings: The paper finds that in a spatial public goods game with diverse punishing strategies, the highest level of public cooperation is attainable through a selection mechanism among punishers. The evolutionary success of a punishing strategy depends on its invasion velocity relative to defectors and other punishers. At low multiplication factors (difficult environments), cooperation among punishing strategies can allow otherwise weak punishers to survive. At higher multiplication factors, competition among punishers can lead to a single dominant strategy. - source: García, J., & Traulsen, A. (2012). Leaving the loners alone: Evolution of cooperation in the presence of antisocial punishment. *Journal of Theoretical Biology*.

  findings: The paper finds that the evolutionary success of cooperation and punishment in public goods games with voluntary participation depends critically on whether loners (abstainers) can be punished or can punish others. If loners are truly isolated (neither punish nor are punished), cooperators who punish defectors become dominant in the population, even when antisocial punishment is allowed. If loners can be punished, cooperation and punishment do not evolve, and the population is split among cooperators, defectors, and loners, with no strategy dominating. The results are robust across different strategy sets and selection intensities. However, the paper does not report group efficiency or total payoff; instead, it focuses on the abundance of strategies as the main outcome.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides strong theoretical evidence that the ability to punish or be punished, especially for abstainers (loners), is a critical moderator of whether punishment can support cooperation in public goods games. For prediction tasks, the findings suggest that if the game design allows abstainers to be punished, punishment is unlikely to increase efficiency or cooperation. If abstainers are truly isolated, punishment can support the dominance of cooperative strategies. However, because the paper does not report efficiency or group payoff, its direct value for predicting efficiency outcomes is limited. The results are most useful for understanding which game design features (especially the treatment of abstainers) are likely to enable or undermine the effectiveness of punishment in promoting cooperation.

Theoretical models show that optimal (time-varying) incentive protocols can minimize the cumulative cost required to reach a desired cooperation level. Punishment is generally more cost-effective than reward for achieving high cooperation. Adaptive hybrid strategies (first carrot, then stick) can outperform pure punishment or reward. The paper also highlights that the structure of the population and the design of the incentive protocol (e.g., thresholds for switching between punishment and exclusion) are important moderators. However, the main outcomes are cooperation rates and incentive costs, not group efficiency.

It is highly relevant for understanding the mechanisms by which punishment can promote cooperation, and for predicting how design features (such as the presence of punishment, the cost and effectiveness of punishment, and the use of hybrid strategies) might influence cooperation rates. However, because the primary outcomes are cooperation rates and incentive costs, not group efficiency or total payoff, the paper is only indirectly informative for predicting the effect of punishment on efficiency. The models suggest that punishment can increase cooperation and that cost-effective protocols exist, but do not provide direct quantitative predictions of efficiency changes.

  findings: The paper finds that cooperative strategies in public goods games and related social dilemmas are governed by a common conditional rule: cooperate with those of good reputation and enforce (by withholding benefits or costly punishment) against those of bad reputation. The choice between withholding benefits and costly punishment depends on the structure of the game—costly punishment is more relevant in public goods games where defectors cannot be targeted directly. The paper reviews experimental evidence showing that combining costly punishment with indirect reciprocity can increase cooperation at lower cost than punishment alone, but does not provide quantitative efficiency outcomes. Theoretical and experimental evidence suggests that the same reputation rules (e.g., SCORING, SIMPLE STANDING, STERN JUDGING) operate across frameworks.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides theoretical and qualitative support for the idea that the effectiveness of punishment in increasing cooperation (and potentially efficiency) in public goods games depends on whether withholding benefits is a viable enforcement mechanism. It suggests that costly punishment is most effective and necessary in public goods games where direct targeting of defectors is not possible. However, the paper does not provide quantitative data on efficiency or payoff outcomes, so it cannot be used directly to predict treatment efficiency from game design dimensions and control efficiency. It is most useful for understanding the conditions under which punishment is likely to be effective as an enforcement mechanism, and for mapping the conceptual relationships between different enforcement strategies.

Delegation of punishment power and the use of centralized or third-party punishment mechanisms can help sustain cooperation. The paper does not provide direct evidence or quantitative findings about efficiency or group payoff, but it synthesizes behavioral mechanisms that are relevant to the prediction of such outcomes.

For prediction tasks, this paper supports the idea that the effect of punishment on efficiency is likely to be moderated by factors such as the structure of punishment (individual vs. centralized), the possibility of retaliation, and the availability of reward. - source: Duong, M. H., Durbac, C. M., & Han, T. A. (2024). Cost Optimisation of Individual-Based Institutional Reward Incentives for Promoting Cooperation in Finite Populations. *Bulletin of Mathematical Biology*.

  findings: The paper finds that the expected total cost to the institution for achieving a target cooperation level in finite-population PGGs depends strongly on the threshold for incentive application (t), the strength of selection (β), mutation rate (μ), and the type of incentive (reward, punishment, hybrid). For small thresholds (t=1), the cost function is always non-decreasing in the per-capita incentive cost, and explicit formulas are derived. For larger thresholds, the cost function can exhibit non-monotonic behavior and phase transitions, especially at high selection strength. Numerical results show that both reward and punishment incentives can be optimized for cost, but the optimal cost and its behavior depend on the game parameters and incentive scheme. The paper provides a framework for predicting the institutional cost required to achieve a desired cooperation level, given the game design and population parameters.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides theoretical and numerical evidence on how the cost of institutional incentives (reward, punishment, hybrid) required to achieve a target cooperation level in PGG-like environments depends on game design dimensions such as player count, group size, marginal per-capita return, and the structure of the incentive scheme (threshold t, cost per unit, effectiveness). While the main outcome is the institutional cost rather than group efficiency, the results are directly relevant for predicting how changes in punishment or reward design (e.g., cost, threshold, effectiveness) will affect the efficiency of institutional intervention. The paper is most informative for settings where the goal is to optimize the cost of achieving cooperation, rather than to maximize group payoff per se. It provides explicit formulas and numerical results that can be used to inform predictions about the efficiency of punishment or reward interventions, conditional on game design and baseline cooperation levels.

- source: Murase, Y., & Baek, S. K. (2021). Friendly-rivalry solution to the iterated n-person public-goods game. *Plos Computational Biology*.

  findings: The paper finds that the CAPRI-n strategy achieves full cooperation and maximal efficiency in the iterated n-person public-goods game, even with implementation errors. When all players use CAPRI-n, the group achieves the cooperative payoff in the limit of small error probability. The strategy is defensible (cannot be exploited), efficient (achieves full cooperation), and distinguishable (can exploit unconditional cooperators). Evolutionary simulations show that CAPRI-n dominates the population across a wide range of benefit-to-cost ratios and population sizes, outperforming other memory-one strategies. The results are robust for n=2 and 3, and supported by Monte Carlo simulation for n=4.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides strong theoretical and simulation-based evidence that, in repeated public-goods games with error, a well-designed punishment/reciprocity strategy (CAPRI-n) can achieve near-maximal efficiency, even as group size increases. The findings suggest that, when the game allows for memory-based contingent punishment and recovery, enabling such mechanisms can dramatically increase efficiency relative to baseline. The results are most directly applicable to settings with continuous contributions, no explicit punishment cost, and no external punishment/reward mechanism, but where strategies can implement contingent retaliation. The paper is highly informative for predicting efficiency in repeated PGGs with endogenous, strategy-based punishment/reciprocity, especially as group size increases.

  findings: Adaptive rewarding in spatial public goods games can eliminate defectors and promote high levels of cooperation, outperforming steady (non-adaptive) rewarding. The effectiveness of adaptive rewarding depends on the synergy factor (r), the cost of rewarding (alpha), and the strength of the reward (Delta). When rewards are strong and not too costly, adaptive rewarding can lead to defector-free states, interpreted as maximal efficiency. However, adaptive punishment is even more effective: for the same cost, punishment achieves defector elimination at lower required intensity. The paper provides detailed phase diagrams showing under what parameter regimes each strategy dominates, coexists, or is eliminated. The main efficiency outcome is the prevalence of defector-free states, which is used as a proxy for group welfare.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides strong theoretical evidence that, in spatial public goods games, adaptive punishment is more effective than adaptive rewarding at achieving maximal efficiency (defector-free states), given the same cost-to-impact ratio. The results are highly informative for predicting the effect of introducing punishment (or reward) in spatial PGGs: punishment is more likely to yield higher efficiency than reward, especially when the cost of sanctioning is not prohibitive. The findings are most directly applicable to spatial, lattice-based PGGs with local interactions, and may be less directly transferable to well-mixed or non-spatial settings. The paper's phase diagrams and minimum required cost-to-impact ratios for defector elimination can inform quantitative predictions about efficiency under different game design parameters.

Mutation (strategy exploration) can synergistically interact with global exclusion, further increasing the emergent level of cooperation and efficiency, with an optimal mutation rate maximizing this effect. The model also identifies bifurcation structures and regions of parameter space where global exclusion is most effective.

The effect is robust to the presence of unbiased mutation (strategy exploration), and there is an optimal mutation rate that maximizes efficiency. For prediction tasks, the findings suggest that, given a control game without exclusion/punishment, enabling a global exclusion mechanism (with reasonable cost) will increase average efficiency, and that the effect is further enhanced by moderate levels of mutation/exploration. The results are most directly applicable to infinitely well-mixed, large-population, one-shot or non-repeated PGGs with centralized exclusion and no second-order free-riding.   findings: The paper finds that in a multi-player public goods game, honest signaling of quality by providing a public good (or by punishing defectors) can be an evolutionarily stable strategy, provided that the cost of signaling is lower for high-quality individuals and that the benefits of alliances or partnerships are sufficiently high. The signaling equilibrium yields higher average group payoffs than the non-signaling equilibrium. The model also shows that punishment can function as a costly signal, and that under certain conditions, prosocial signals (including punishment) are more likely to evolve than neutral or antisocial signals. The model provides explicit conditions for when signaling equilibria exist and are stable, and analyzes the evolutionary dynamics leading to these equilibria.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides strong theoretical support for the idea that enabling costly signaling (including punishment) in public goods games can increase group efficiency and average payoff, even in the absence of repeated interactions or reciprocity. The model is directly relevant to predicting the effect of punishment on efficiency, especially in settings where punishment is interpreted as a costly signal of quality. The findings suggest that, when the cost structure and benefit parameters are appropriate, introducing punishment (as a form of signaling) should increase efficiency relative to a control without punishment. The paper also highlights the importance of the cost differential between high- and low-quality individuals, the size of the group, and the benefits of alliances in determining the stability and efficiency of the signaling equilibrium. However, as a theoretical model, it does not provide empirical effect sizes or direct experimental evidence.

  findings: The paper finds that introducing a global exclusion mechanism (a centralized institution that can exclude defectors from the public good) into the public goods game can lead to higher efficiency and average group payoff, provided the cost of exclusion is not too high and the probability of successful exclusion is sufficiently large. The model predicts that, in these parameter regions, cooperation can emerge and be stabilized, sometimes through cyclic dominance among defectors, cooperators, and excluders. The results are robust across a wide range of functional forms for the exclusion probability. When exclusion is too costly or too unlikely, the system reverts to defection and low efficiency. The paper does not analyze empirical data but provides theoretical and numerical phase diagrams supporting these conclusions.

The effect is robust to the details of how exclusion is implemented, as long as the exclusion probability is high enough and the cost is not prohibitive. For prediction tasks, this suggests that, when the game design includes a global exclusion mechanism with moderate or low cost and high effectiveness, one should expect a significant increase in efficiency relative to the control. The model also clarifies that if exclusion is too costly or ineffective, efficiency gains will not materialize. The findings are directly relevant for predicting the efficiency impact of institutional punishment/exclusion in PGG-like environments.

- source: Liu, L. J., & Chen, X. J. (2020). Evolutionary game dynamics in multiagent systems with prosocial and antisocial exclusion strategies. *Knowledge-based Systems*.
  type: theory | empirical=N/A | experimental=N/A
  relevance: pgg=exact | punishment=close | payoff=exact
  outcomes: primary=efficiency_or_payoff | overall_effect=more_positive
  dimensions: player_count, num_rounds, mpcr, punishment_cost, punishment_tech
  findings: The paper shows that in finite well-mixed populations playing a public goods game, prosocial pool exclusion (where cooperators can pay to exclude defectors from benefits) is more effective at promoting cooperation and group efficiency than costly punishment. Even when antisocial exclusion (where defectors exclude cooperators) is introduced, prosocial pool excluders maintain their evolutionary advantage and can dominate the population, especially when second-order sanctioning is allowed. When both exclusion and punishment (prosocial and antisocial) are available, prosocial pool excluders prevail and maximize group payoff/efficiency. Antisocial exclusion alone leads to defection and low efficiency, but does not undermine the effectiveness of prosocial exclusion when both are present.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides strong theoretical evidence that, in public goods games with the option for prosocial exclusion, enabling such exclusion mechanisms leads to higher group efficiency and welfare than enabling costly punishment, even in the presence of antisocial sanctioning. The results are robust to the inclusion of second-order sanctioning and to moderate changes in the marginal per-capita return (mpcr). For prediction tasks, the presence of prosocial exclusion as a punishment-like mechanism should be expected to increase efficiency relative to control, and to outperform standard costly punishment. The findings are most directly applicable to games with continuous contributions, no communication, and fixed group size and rounds, as modeled here.

- source: Xie, K., & Liu, T. J. (2024). The regulation of good and evi promotes cooperation in public goods game. *Applied Mathematics and Computation*.

  findings: The paper finds that allowing players to both punish defectors and reward cooperators (PEPG strategy) in a spatial public goods game, especially when combined with heterogeneous payoff allocation based on reputation, leads to higher cooperation rates and higher average payoffs for cooperators. The effect is sensitive to the enhancement factor (r), the importance of reputation in payoff allocation (a), and the strength of the bonus-penalty (gamma). Defectors' average payoffs are always lower than those of cooperators in the steady state. The model demonstrates that the union of PEPG and reputation-based heterogeneity is more effective than either alone.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides simulation evidence that combining punishment and reward (PEPG) with reputation-based heterogeneous payoffs increases cooperation and average payoffs in public goods games. For prediction tasks, the results suggest that enabling punishment (especially when combined with reward and reputation mechanisms) will increase efficiency, particularly when the marginal per-capita return (mpcr, via r), the effectiveness of punishment/reward (gamma), and the importance of reputation (a) are high. However, the model is not a direct empirical test and does not report efficiency as a ratio to the fully cooperative optimum, so quantitative predictions should be made with caution.

  findings: The paper finds that social exclusion mechanisms (peer and pool) can allow excluders to dominate over defectors in finite-population public goods games, depending on exclusion cost, group size, and exclusion effectiveness. Peer exclusion is more effective at low costs, while pool exclusion is more robust at high costs and larger group sizes. Both mechanisms can sustain cooperation and prevent the dominance of defectors, which would otherwise reduce group payoff. The analysis is based on evolutionary game theory, using payoff functions and fixation probabilities, rather than direct simulation of group efficiency. The results suggest that enabling exclusion mechanisms can improve group outcomes compared to no-punishment baselines, especially under the right parameter conditions.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides theoretical support that enabling exclusion-based punishment in public goods games can increase the prevalence of cooperation and, by implication, group efficiency, especially when exclusion is effective and/or costs are not too high. The results are parameterized by group size, exclusion cost, and exclusion probability, and show that pool exclusion is more robust in large groups or at high costs. While the paper does not report efficiency as a direct outcome, the dominance of excluders and cooperators over defectors implies higher group payoff. For prediction tasks, the findings suggest that the effect of punishment on efficiency will be more positive when exclusion is effective, costs are moderate, and group size is not too large for peer exclusion (but pool exclusion can handle larger groups). However, the lack of direct efficiency reporting and the theoretical nature of the results mean that quantitative predictions should be made with caution.

Migration costs (punishment) robustly increase average contribution, especially at low enhancement factors, and are more effective than rewards. The combined mechanism can further improve cooperation in some cases. The main reported outcome is average contribution, not efficiency or group payoff. The results suggest that institutional punishment (here, migration cost) is a stronger driver of cooperation than institutional rewards in this spatial setting.

The findings are most useful for understanding how migration costs and rewards affect contribution rates under different enhancement factors, group sizes, and migration probabilities. For prediction tasks focused on efficiency, this paper offers only adjacent, indirect support.

- source: Wang, X. J., Ding, R., Zhao, J. H., & Gu, C. L. (2022). The rise and fall of cooperation in populations with multiple groups. *Applied Mathematics and Computation*.
  type: theory | empirical=N/A | experimental=N/A

  findings: The presence of inequity-averse individuals (both punishers and rewarders) can promote the survival of contributors and the elimination of defectors in spatial public goods games, but the effectiveness depends on the synergy factor (r), the cost (alpha), and the intensity (beta) of punishment/reward. First-order inequity aversion (punishment) is more effective at low r, while second-order (reward) is more effective at high r. Increasing the cost of punishment/reward (alpha) undermines the effect of punishment more than reward. Increasing the intensity (beta) generally promotes cooperation, but can also lead to cyclic dominance phases where defectors persist. The model shows that the traditional result that punishment is more effective than reward does not always hold when punishment/reward is based on payoff inequity rather than strategy. However, the paper does not report efficiency or group payoff outcomes, so implications for efficiency are indirect.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides indirect evidence about how punishment and reward mechanisms, when based on payoff inequity rather than strategy, affect the prevalence of cooperation in spatial public goods games. It suggests that the effectiveness of punishment and reward depends on the synergy factor, cost, and intensity, and that the relationship is non-monotonic and context-dependent. However, because the paper does not report efficiency or group payoff outcomes, it does not directly inform predictions about the effect of punishment on efficiency. The results are most relevant for understanding how design dimensions like mpcr (r), punishment/reward cost and effectiveness, and the presence of reward interact to affect the prevalence of cooperation, but not directly the efficiency.

The findings suggest that exclusion-based punishment can be a powerful mechanism for sustaining cooperation, but the paper does not provide direct evidence on efficiency or payoff outcomes.

However, because the paper does not report efficiency, group payoff, or welfare, it cannot be used directly to predict the effect of punishment on efficiency. The findings are most useful for predicting the effect of punishment on cooperation rates, and only indirectly suggest that efficiency may increase when cooperation is high. Importantly, even without punishment (compensation), cooperation can persist within effective agreements due to clustering of conditional cooperators. However, the paper does not report on group efficiency or total payoff, so the direct effect of punishment on efficiency is not established.

  findings: The study finds that punishing the minority strategy in each group (regardless of whether it is cooperation or defection) can strongly promote the emergence of cooperation in a spatial public goods game. As the punishment fine increases, the fraction of cooperators rises, and for high punishment, the system can abruptly transition from full defection to full cooperation as the multiplication factor increases. Theoretical analysis shows that the payoff difference between cooperators and defectors increases with punishment severity, favoring the expansion of cooperator clusters. However, the paper does not report group efficiency or total payoff, so the effect of this punishment rule on overall welfare or efficiency remains unclear.

However, because the main outcome is cooperation rate and not efficiency or group payoff, the findings should be used with caution for predicting efficiency outcomes. Theoretical payoff differences are provided, but without explicit efficiency or welfare analysis, it is unclear whether the increased cooperation translates to higher group efficiency, especially given the costs of punishment. The paper is most informative for predicting cooperation rates under minority punishment rules, but less so for efficiency predictions required by the downstream task.

For prediction tasks, the results suggest that introducing a well-calibrated incentive mechanism (with moderate cost and effectiveness) can increase group efficiency relative to a control without such mechanisms. However, the findings are based on simulation, not empirical data, and may not transfer directly to real-world or experimental PGGs with punishment.

The findings suggest that, in the absence of punishment, reward alone is insufficient to fully stabilize cooperation and maximize efficiency.   findings: The paper finds that institutional intervention, modeled as a central authority forcing some defectors to contribute, can increase the efficiency (average total payoff) of a spatial PGG, especially when the synergy factor is high and the intervention cost is controlled. Weak intervention can paradoxically reduce cooperation and efficiency, but moderate intervention can lead to higher group incomes than the standard PGG. Excessive intervention may reduce cooperation. The effect of intervention is distinct from peer punishment, as the cost is shared by all contributors and there is no direct punisher. The effect is non-monotonic: weak or excessive intervention can reduce efficiency. The findings suggest that, when predicting the effect of punishment-like interventions on efficiency, one should consider the strength and cost of the intervention and the underlying mpcr. - source: Kurokawa, S., & Ihara, Y. (2017). Evolution of group-wise cooperation: Is direct reciprocity insufficient?. *Journal of Theoretical Biology*.
  type: theory | empirical=N/A | experimental=N/A

  findings: The paper shows that in n-player repeated prisoners' dilemma games with non-rivalrous public goods, direct reciprocity alone can support the evolution of cooperation (and thus high group efficiency), especially as group size increases. This holds even when individuals sometimes make mistakes or have imperfect information, provided they use sufficiently optimistic conditional strategies. The analysis is entirely theoretical and does not include punishment or reward mechanisms. The main outcome is the condition under which cooperative strategies are selectively favored over defection, which is directly tied to group payoff and efficiency. The paper does not provide empirical or simulated efficiency values, but gives analytic thresholds for when cooperation is favored.

However, the paper does not model punishment, so it does not provide direct evidence for the effect of enabling punishment on efficiency. Its results are most relevant for predicting efficiency in control (no-punishment) conditions as a function of group size, information, and error, but not for the effect of punishment. The paper is useful for understanding baseline efficiency in repeated public goods games with direct reciprocity, but not for predicting the incremental effect of punishment.

- source: Sasaki, T., & Unemi, T. (2011). Replicator dynamics in public goods games with reward funds. *Journal of Theoretical Biology*.
  type: theory | empirical=N/A | experimental=N/A
  relevance: pgg=exact | punishment=adjacent | payoff=exact
  outcomes: primary=efficiency_or_payoff | overall_effect=more_positive
  dimensions: player_count, num_rounds, mpcr, reward_exists, reward_cost, reward_tech
  findings: The paper finds that in a compulsory public goods game with a pool-rewarding mechanism, cooperation and high efficiency can be maintained if the net benefit from the reward fund exceeds the cost of contributing to the public good. Specifically, if c2*(r2-1) > sigma (where sigma is the net cost of contributing to the public good), the population can converge to all rewarders (full efficiency) or exhibit stable cycles with high average payoff. If this condition is not met, defectors dominate and efficiency collapses. The model also shows that introducing second-order sanctions (reducing rewards to second-order free riders) can stabilize full cooperation. The findings are directly relevant to predicting efficiency in PGG-like games with reward mechanisms, but only indirectly inform about punishment.
  prediction_guidance: This paper provides strong theoretical evidence that, in public goods games with reward funds, the efficiency outcome depends critically on the relative effectiveness and cost of the reward mechanism compared to the cost of cooperation. The explicit condition c2*(r2-1) > sigma can be used to predict when enabling a reward mechanism will increase efficiency relative to the control (no reward) case. However, the paper does not analyze punishment, so its direct value for predicting the effect of punishment on efficiency is limited. The model structure and results may be informative by analogy for understanding how the cost and effectiveness of sanctions (punishment or reward) interact with game parameters (group size, MPCR, etc.) to determine efficiency outcomes.
